title: 2 Kings 4:8–17
context: A prominent woman of Shunem, a town in the territory of Issachar (Joshua 19:18), shows Elisha repeated hospitality and, with her husband’s agreement, builds him a furnished room on the roof. When Elisha seeks to repay her, she declines any appeal to the king or the army commander, content among her own people. Gehazi observes that she has no son and that her husband is old, and Elisha promises that she will embrace a son within a year. She bears a son as promised. Both traditions note the echo of the promise of a son to Sarah (Genesis 18:10–14) and read the birth as an unearned gift of the LORD’s kindness to a generous, discerning woman.

verses.text: One day Elisha went to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread.
verses.arminianNotes: A prominent woman of Shunem persuades Elisha to eat with her, and her hospitality becomes a regular practice whenever he passes by. Arminian readers note her generous initiative, freely offered and sustained over time, as a model of welcoming God’s servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her hospitality as the fruit of a heart God has turned toward his servant and his word. Both traditions agree that the narrator honors this woman’s character, and that ordinary meals become the setting for God’s later blessing on her household.

verses.text: She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually.
verses.arminianNotes: She tells her husband that she perceives Elisha to be a holy man of God. Arminian readers note her spiritual discernment and her desire to act on it, and they see her perception as a genuine response to the evidence of God’s work in his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her recognition of the holy man of God as an insight God has given, leading her to honor the prophet’s calling. Both traditions agree that her discernment and initiative are commendable, and that she acts in partnership with her husband rather than apart from him.

verses.text: Please, let’s make a little room on the roof. Let’s set a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand for him there. When he comes to us, he can stay there.”
verses.arminianNotes: She proposes a small room on the roof with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. Arminian readers highlight the thoughtfulness of her plan, showing practical love that anticipates another’s needs and makes room for God’s servant in her home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that her generosity seeks nothing in return, reflecting the free kindness that marks those touched by God’s grace. Both traditions agree that the furnished room is a concrete act of hospitality that the narrative remembers with honor and that will become central to the story ahead.

verses.text: One day he came there, and he went to the room and lay there.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha comes and rests in the room she prepared. Arminian readers note that her hospitality is received, and that the prepared room becomes the place where Elisha considers how to bless her in return for her faithful kindness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ordinary moment of rest as the occasion God uses to bring blessing into her household. Both traditions agree that the narrative moves quietly from the woman’s generosity to the prophet’s response, which will reveal God’s care for her in a way she did not seek.

verses.text: He said to Gehazi his servant, “Call this Shunammite.” When he had called her, she stood before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha asks Gehazi his servant to call the Shunammite, and she stands before him. Arminian readers note that the prophet wants to respond personally to her kindness, and that Gehazi is introduced here as a servant who will play a significant role in the story to come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Elisha’s initiative reflects the LORD’s attentiveness to those who serve his people. Both traditions agree that the scene sets up a conversation in which gratitude seeks to express itself in blessing, and that the woman is treated with respect.

verses.text: He said to him, “Say now to her, ‘Behold, you have cared for us with all this care. What is to be done for you? Would you like to be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the army?’ ” She answered, “I dwell among my own people.”
verses.arminianNotes: Through Gehazi, Elisha offers to speak for her to the king or the captain of the army, but she replies that she dwells among her own people. Arminian readers see contentment in her answer, noting that she declines worldly influence and finds her security within her community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise admire her contentment and see in it a heart that does not seek favor from the powerful. Both traditions agree that her answer reveals settled dignity, and that the narrative honors her for offering hospitality without expecting any reward.

verses.text: He said, “What then is to be done for her?” Gehazi answered, “Most certainly she has no son, and her husband is old.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi points out that she has no son and that her husband is old. Arminian readers note that the observation surfaces an unspoken need, and that God’s blessing will meet her at the point of her deepest, unvoiced longing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s attention to a need she did not mention, demonstrating that the LORD knows and provides beyond what his people ask. Both traditions agree that childlessness in the ancient world carried real sorrow and insecurity, and that the story moves toward God’s gracious answer.

verses.text: He said, “Call her.” When he had called her, she stood in the door.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha calls her, and she stands in the doorway. Arminian readers note the respectful distance she keeps and see her as a woman responding to God’s servant with humility and openness to whatever word he may speak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the moment as the threshold of God’s promise, as the prophet prepares to announce what only God can give. Both traditions agree that the narrative slows here to heighten the significance of the word that follows, drawing attention to the woman’s place in the story.

verses.text: He said, “At this season next year, you will embrace a son.” She said, “No, my lord, you man of God, do not lie to your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha promises that she will embrace a son by this season next year, and she pleads with him not to lie to her. Arminian readers hear in her response the protective caution of someone who has lived with disappointment, and they note that God’s promise meets her honest fear with grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise as a sovereign gift, echoing God’s promise of a son to Sarah (Genesis 18:10–14). Both traditions agree that her reply does not disqualify her from the blessing, and that the LORD’s promises often come to people whose hope has been long tested.

verses.text: The woman conceived, and bore a son at that season when the time came around, as Elisha had said to her.
verses.arminianNotes: She conceives and bears a son at the appointed season, as Elisha said. Arminian readers note the faithfulness of God’s word and the joy of a long-awaited gift, and they see her hospitality and trust honored in the birth of her child.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the birth occurs exactly as the prophet announced, displaying God’s sovereign power over life and his faithfulness to his word. Both traditions agree that the child is a gift of grace rather than a payment earned, and that the LORD fulfills what he promises.
